```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 120)
library(cdzoo)
has_pcalg <- requireNamespace("pcalg", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_proxymix <- requireNamespace("proxymix", quietly = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
```

`cdzoo` puts a portfolio of causal-discovery algorithms behind one interface. The
R ecosystem has strong individual packages -- `pcalg`, `bnlearn` -- but no single
harness that wraps R *and* Python algorithms in one convention with a scenario
grid and fair metrics. `cdzoo` fills that gap: a registry of methods, a grid of
structural-causal-model scenarios with known ground truth, graph-recovery
metrics, and an evidence-routed recommender that suggests a method for a given
data set and says why.

Every back-end is optional. The registry, the scenarios, the metrics, and the
recommender's routing logic all run on a base installation; a method is run only
when its package or Python module is present.

## One interface

`list_methods()` shows the registered methods and which back-ends are installed:

```{r registry}
methods <- list_methods()
methods[, c("id", "name", "family", "language", "installed")]
```

`cd_discover()` runs one method and returns the recovered graph in a single
adjacency convention (the `pcalg` `amat.cpdag` convention, where `graph[i, j]`
is one for a directed edge from `i` to `j`, and both `graph[i, j]` and
`graph[j, i]` are one for an unoriented edge):

```{r discover, eval = has_pcalg}
sim <- cd_scenario("linear_gaussian", seed = 1)
res <- cd_discover(sim$data, "pc_pcalg")
res
head(cd_edges(res))
```

## The recommender

Causal discovery has no run-time ground truth, so `cd_auto()` is a recommender,
not a selector: it inspects the data, routes the problem to a method suited to
that regime, runs the best installed method on the route, and reports its
rationale and a confidence label. `cd_diagnose()` shows the transparent
characteristics it reads:

```{r diagnose}
cd_diagnose(cd_scenario("linear_laplace", seed = 1)$data)
```

```{r recommend}
rec <- cd_auto(cd_scenario("linear_laplace", seed = 1)$data, report = FALSE)
rec@method
rec@rationale
rec@confidence
```

The routing follows the benchmark evidence below. The signature each test reads
maps to a method family the benchmark shows is suited to it:

| Data signature | Routed to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Markedly non-Gaussian margins | `icalingam_pcalg` / `directlingam_py` | non-Gaussianity identifies orientation; the LiNGAM family is fast and accurate |
| A nonlinear-mechanism heuristic | `pc_kci_cl` | a kernel conditional-independence test handles nonlinear dependence |
| Near-singular covariance | `fci_pcalg` / `rcd_py` | a hint of latent structure; a confounder-robust method is safer |
| Approximately Gaussian, comparable residual variances | `golem_gcastle` / `dagma_linear_py` | the continuous-optimisation methods exploit equal-variance identifiability |
| No decisive signature | `golem_gcastle` | the strongest method overall in the benchmark |

When unsure, `mode = "consensus"` runs the top routed methods and returns their
stability-weighted union with per-edge agreement:

```{r consensus, eval = has_pcalg}
lap <- cd_scenario("linear_laplace", seed = 1)
con <- cd_auto(lap$data, mode = "consensus", top_k = 2)
con@method
head(cd_edges(con))
```

## The benchmark evidence

`cd_field_benchmark` is a summary of sixteen established methods run across nine
structural-causal-model scenarios, each scored against its known DAG. It is the
evidence behind the recommender's routing. The overall ranking by mean structural
Hamming distance -- the number of single-edge edits between the estimate and the
truth, so lower is better:

```{r ranking}
agg <- aggregate(cbind(shd, skeleton_f1, runtime_s) ~ method_name + family,
                 data = cd_field_benchmark, FUN = mean)
agg <- agg[order(agg$shd), ]
agg$shd <- round(agg$shd, 2)
agg$skeleton_f1 <- round(agg$skeleton_f1, 3)
agg$runtime_s <- round(agg$runtime_s, 3)
agg
```

The continuous-optimisation family leads on these regimes, the LiNGAM family is
the strongest accuracy-per-millisecond entrant, and the kernel and search methods
trail on the linear scenarios while staying available for the nonlinear ones.

```{r fig-accuracy, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.alt = "Mean structural Hamming distance by method, lower is better, coloured by algorithm family."}
library(ggplot2)
ord <- agg[order(-agg$shd), "method_name"]
plot_df <- agg
plot_df$method_name <- factor(plot_df$method_name, levels = ord)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(method_name, shd, fill = family)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mean structural Hamming distance (lower is better)",
       fill = "family",
       title = "Discovery accuracy across nine scenarios") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r fig-speed, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.alt = "Mean runtime against mean structural Hamming distance, the speed-accuracy trade-off, on a logarithmic runtime axis."}
ggplot(agg, aes(runtime_s, shd, colour = family, label = method_name)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "mean runtime (seconds, log scale)",
       y = "mean structural Hamming distance",
       colour = "family",
       title = "The speed-accuracy trade-off") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Score your own runs

`cd_scenario()` realises a scenario at a seed with its true graph attached, and
`cd_score()` scores a recovered graph against it with skeleton F1, structural
Hamming distance, and orientation recall:

```{r score, eval = has_pcalg}
sim <- cd_scenario("linear_bimodal", seed = 2)
cd_score(cd_discover(sim$data, "icalingam_pcalg"), sim$truth)
```

`cd_benchmark()` runs the grid for you, isolating each run so a back-end that
fails on a cell records a status rather than stopping the sweep:

```{r benchmark, eval = has_pcalg}
cd_benchmark(methods = c("pc_pcalg", "ges_pcalg"),
             scenarios = c("linear_gaussian", "linear_bimodal"),
             seeds = 1:2, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Structure from an evaluable density

The sampling-based methods need a sample. When a density can be evaluated but not
sampled -- it is given as a mixture or an energy model rather than draws -- the
conditional-independence (Markov) structure can be read off the mixture in closed
form instead. Passing a `proxymix` mixture or target to `cd_auto()` takes this
route:

```{r density, eval = has_proxymix}
# a three-variable mixture whose precision makes x1 and x3 conditionally
# independent given x2 -- a chain x1 -- x2 -- x3
sigma <- solve(matrix(c(1, -0.5, 0, -0.5, 1.25, -0.5, 0, -0.5, 1), 3, 3))
g <- proxymix::gmm(weights = 1, means = list(c(0, 0, 0)),
                   covariances = list(sigma))
res <- cd_auto(g)
res@rationale
cd_edges(res)
```

This is the case no sampling-based method in the registry can serve, and it is
why the recommender accepts a density as well as a data matrix.
